steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a survey paper on AI-powered fraud detection in decentralized finance (DeFi), which organizes frauds and detection methods by the stages of a DeFi project's life cycle.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- DeFi growth and the rise of fraud
- AI for fraud detection in DeFi; need for a survey
- Gaps in existing surveys
- Our life-cycle taxonomy
- Highlights of findings
- Paper organization

  - Dune: unique addresses over 42 million as of July 2023, up from 20 million at start of 2022

  - Figure 1: from Mt. Gox hack in 2011 to 2023 February, big increase
  - 231 DeFi hacks, 135 security attacks, 95 fraudulent schemes; approx $16.7 billion stolen over 12 years
  - need to study and detect -> more trustworthy ecosystem
- AI for fraud detection
  - AI potential for complex fraud detection problems; publicly available data
  - ML (tree-based, deep learning): classify suspicious transactions, identify fraudsters
  - NLP: whitepapers, social media posts, smart contract code
  - statistical modeling, network analysis
  - -> survey needed: collect methods, review effectiveness, gaps, future directions
- Gaps in existing work
  - no systematic taxonomy of fraud across the whole ecosystem
  - previous literature: cryptocurrency markets only, overlooks other components
  - NFT: unique, non-fungible, no standardized pricing, reshapes market dynamics
  - DEX: less-regulated, decentralized smart-contract framework, vulnerable
  - new frauds: rug pulls, DEX hacks; old scams in new forms: phishing, wash trading
  - some surveys cover countermeasures for individual frauds, no holistic view or classification
  - frauds still evolving, lots of AI research, but no systematic survey -> motivation
- Taxonomy
  - Product Life Cycle Theory: five stages - development, introduction, growth, maturity, decline
  - frauds correlate with project stage
  - (1) development: lack of oversight/security -> investment traps, Ponzi schemes, rug pulls
  - (2) introduction and growth: market manipulation, wash trading, insider trading, less-regulated

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Blockchain technology has developed rapidly, and decentralized finance (DeFi) has become an emerging alternative to deal with the challenges of traditional finance (CeFi) systems. CeFi relies on intermediaries in a centralized system for transactions. DeFi instead uses distributed ledger technology, smart contracts, and a wide range of decentralized apps (DApps) so that global, peer-to-peer financial activities are possible, and it eliminates traditional intermediaries for transparency and efficiency. According to Dune, the number of unique addresses in DeFi has gone up to over 42 million as of July 2023, compared to 20 million addresses at the start of 2022. But as DeFi gets more popular, fraudulent activities in the DeFi ecosystem have also surged. They pose significant risks and erode trust, and they impact both individual users and the whole DeFi community. Figure 1 shows that DeFi fraud has increased a lot from the first crypto exchange hack (Mt. Gox) in 2011 up until 2023 February. In total 231 DeFi hacks, 135 security attacks, and 95 fraudulent schemes have been reported, and approximately $16.7 billion in cryptocurrencies were stolen over 12 years. So it is important to study these frauds and develop effective methods to detect them, to make the DeFi ecosystem more trustworthy.

At the same time as fraud has been rising, advancements in Artificial Intelligence (AI) have shown great potential for complex fraud detection problems in recent years. Researchers have used these technologies to improve fraud detection in the DeFi ecosystem with publicly available data. Machine learning models, like tree-based and deep learning approaches, have been used to classify suspicious transactions and identify potential fraudsters. Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques have been used to analyze text from project whitepapers, social media posts, and the code of smart contracts. Other technologies like statistical modeling and network analysis have also been used to identify frauds in DeFi. So a comprehensive survey is needed to collect the existing fraud detection methods, review how effective they are, identify gaps, and give insights into future research directions.

- gaps: no systematic taxonomy of fraud across ecosystem; previous literature on cryptocurrency markets only; NFT (unique, non-fungible, no standardized pricing); DEX (less-regulated, vulnerable); new frauds (rug pulls, DEX hacks), old scams in new forms (phishing, wash trading); surveys on individual frauds lack holistic view -> motivation
- taxonomy: Product Life Cycle Theory, five stages (development, introduction, growth, maturity, decline); (1) development: Ponzi schemes, rug pulls; (2) introduction/growth: wash trading, insider trading; (3) maturity/decline: pump and dump (low-cap), money laundering and phishing (high-cap)
- highlights: Fraud Types and Organizers; Detection Methods; Detection Effectiveness; Future Directions
- organization: Sections 2-10

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Blockchain technology has developed rapidly, and decentralized finance (DeFi) has become an emerging alternative to deal with the challenges of traditional finance (CeFi) systems. CeFi relies on intermediaries in a centralized system for transactions. DeFi instead uses distributed ledger technology, smart contracts, and a wide range of decentralized apps (DApps) so that global, peer-to-peer financial activities are possible, and it eliminates traditional intermediaries for transparency and efficiency. According to Dune, the number of unique addresses in DeFi has gone up to over 42 million as of July 2023, compared to 20 million addresses at the start of 2022. But as DeFi gets more popular, fraudulent activities in the DeFi ecosystem have also surged. They pose significant risks and erode trust, and they impact both individual users and the whole DeFi community. Figure 1 shows that DeFi fraud has increased a lot from the first crypto exchange hack (Mt. Gox) in 2011 up until 2023 February. In total 231 DeFi hacks, 135 security attacks, and 95 fraudulent schemes have been reported, and approximately $16.7 billion in cryptocurrencies were stolen over 12 years. So it is important to study these frauds and develop effective methods to detect them, to make the DeFi ecosystem more trustworthy.

At the same time as fraud has been rising, advancements in Artificial Intelligence (AI) have shown great potential for complex fraud detection problems in recent years. Researchers have used these technologies to improve fraud detection in the DeFi ecosystem with publicly available data. Machine learning models, like tree-based and deep learning approaches, have been used to classify suspicious transactions and identify potential fraudsters. Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques have been used to analyze text from project whitepapers, social media posts, and the code of smart contracts. Other technologies like statistical modeling and network analysis have also been used to identify frauds in DeFi. So a comprehensive survey is needed to collect the existing fraud detection methods, review how effective they are, identify gaps, and give insights into future research directions.

We want to give a comprehensive overview of the current landscape. As far as we know, there is no systematic discussion that gives a comprehensive taxonomy of fraud, and this is crucial to understand DeFi frauds better across the whole ecosystem. Previous literature mostly focused on detecting frauds in cryptocurrency markets and overlooked the frauds in other financial components of the DeFi ecosystem. For example, each Non-Fungible Token (NFT) item is unique and non-fungible, so there is no standardized pricing and the market dynamics are reshaped. Another example is Decentralized Exchange (DEX), which creates a less-regulated realm that is vulnerable to exploitation because of its decentralized, smart contract-driven framework. These components foster new forms of fraud, like rug pulls and DEX hacks, and traditional financial scams like phishing and wash trading take on new forms. Also, some existing surveys have examined countermeasures for individual frauds, but they lack a holistic understanding of what these frauds are and a comprehensive classification methodology. So on one hand various frauds are still evolving in many DeFi projects, and on the other hand a lot of research effort has gone into developing AI-powered fraud detection in DeFi projects. But there is no systematic survey that summarizes those efforts and identifies future research opportunities. This is our motivation to comprehensively survey AI-powered approaches for DeFi fraud detection.

In this survey we present a new methodology for reviewing financial frauds across five stages in the life cycle of DeFi projects, based on the Product Life Cycle Theory: development, introduction, growth, maturity, and decline. The taxonomy is based on our finding that many frauds are strongly correlated with the DeFi project stage. (1) In the project development stage, scammers exploit the lack of oversight and security measures to create investment traps, which leads to fraudulent activities like Ponzi schemes and rug pulls. (2) When the project goes through the introduction and growth stage, dishonest participants can manipulate the market with tactics like wash trading and insider trading because the environment is less regulated. (3) In the maturity and decline stage, low-cap projects become susceptible to pump and dump schemes because market conditions are relatively easier, and high-cap projects face risks like money laundering and phishing scams, which have shown new forms and characteristics in DeFi. The taxonomy gives a systematic categorization of DeFi frauds based on when they occur, and it shows the complex landscape of DeFi frauds.

With this taxonomy our survey gives a comprehensive review of on-chain frauds and of the existing fraud detection methods for frauds at each stage. This leads to some noteworthy findings and potential future directions across the life cycle of DeFi projects. Some highlights are:

- • Fraud Types and Organizers: In the development stage most frauds are investment scams organized by project developers. When projects move to the introduction and growth stages, market manipulations appear. In this phase project developers and DeFi platforms work together to organize fraudulent activities. In the maturity and decline stages the fraud organizers are external entities, who also work with DeFi platforms to organize some market manipulations and new forms of illicit activities.

- • Detection Methods: In the development stage tree-based models are prominent for fraud detection because they have shown superior performance for the small data in this stage. In the introduction and growth stages statistical methods and graph-based patterns are widely used to capture suspicious market activities. Advanced techniques, especially graph-based methods, become prominent in the maturity and decline stages to capture complex relationships in large and complex data.

- • Detection Effectiveness: For frauds in the early stages, fraud detection tasks are still at the beginning. This could be because of limited transaction data and a scarcity of reliable ground truths. Frauds in the later stages have received a lot of attention, and detection performance is good using a large amount of data and advanced models.

- • Future Directions: In the early stages, using pre-trained models and doing early-stage detection can help with proactive fraud prevention. In the later phase researchers can use large language models (LLM) or foundational models to gather more comprehensive information and develop advanced detection techniques. More future directions and open issues for the whole life cycle are also presented in this paper.

The rest of this paper is organized like this. Section 2 gives a background on DeFi frauds and Section 3 our motivation for this survey. Section 4 presents a DeFi fraud taxonomy and an overview of detection methods. Sections 5, 6 and 7 review stage-specific frauds and detection methods. Section 8 presents discussion and findings, and Section 9 discusses potential future directions. Section 10 concludes the paper.

Yet, with its increasing popularity, fraudulent activities in the DeFi ecosystem have surged, posing significant risks and eroding trust for both individual users and the entire DeFi community. As shown in Figure 1, DeFi fraud has increased significantly from the first crypto exchange hack (Mt. Gox) in 2011 up until 2023 February. In total, 231 DeFi hacks, 135 security attacks, and 95 fraudulent schemes have been reported, resulting in approximately $16.7 billion in stolen cryptocurrencies over the span of 12 years [2]. This emphasizes the importance of studying these frauds and developing effective methods to detect them, in order to create a more trustworthy DeFi ecosystem.

With rising fraud activities, advancements in Artificial Intelligence (AI) have shown great potential in tackling complex fraud detection problems in recent years. Researchers have used these technologies to enhance fraud detection within the DeFi ecosystem using publicly available data. Machine learning models, such as tree-based and deep learning approaches, have been applied to classify suspicious transactions [3,4] and identify potential fraudsters [5,6]. Meanwhile, Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques have been employed to analyze textual information from project whitepapers [7], social media posts [8], and the code of smart contracts [9,10]. Other technologies, such as statistical modeling [11] and network analysis [12], have also been used to identify frauds within DeFi. Hence, a comprehensive survey is needed to collect existing fraud detection methods, review their effectiveness, identify gaps, and provide insights into future research directions.

We aim to provide a comprehensive overview of the current landscape. To the best of our knowledge, there is no systematic discussion providing a comprehensive taxonomy of fraud, which is crucial for a deeper understanding of DeFi frauds across the entire ecosystem. Previous literature [13,14,15] has mainly focused on detecting frauds in cryptocurrency markets, overlooking the frauds that occur in other financial components of the DeFi ecosystem. For example, each Non-Fungible Token (NFT) item is unique and non-fungible, which results in the absence of standardized pricing and reshapes market dynamics. Another example is Decentralized Exchange (DEX), which creates a less-regulated realm that is vulnerable to exploitation due to its decentralized, smart contract-driven framework. These distinct components foster new forms of fraud, such as rug pulls [16] and DEX hacks [17], while traditional financial scams, such as phishing [18] and wash trading [11], take on new forms. Moreover, while some existing surveys [13,19] have examined countermeasures for individual frauds, they lack a holistic understanding of the nature of these frauds and a comprehensive classification methodology. On the one hand, various frauds are still evolving in many DeFi projects; on the other hand, a lot of research effort has been devoted to developing AI-powered fraud detection in DeFi projects. However, no systematic survey summarizes those efforts and identifies future research opportunities. This motivates us to comprehensively survey AI-powered approaches for DeFi fraud detection.

In this survey, we present a novel methodology for reviewing financial frauds across five stages in the life cycle of DeFi projects, based on the Product Life Cycle Theory [20]: development, introduction, growth, maturity, and decline. This taxonomy is based on our finding that many frauds are strongly correlated with the DeFi project stage. Specifically, (1) in the project development stage, scammers exploit the lack of oversight and security measures to create investment traps, leading to fraudulent activities like Ponzi schemes [21] and rug pulls [16]. (2) As the project progresses through the introduction and growth stage, dishonest participants can manipulate the market using tactics such as wash trading [22] and insider trading [23] due to the less-regulated environment. (3) In the maturity and decline stage, low-cap projects become susceptible to pump and dump schemes [24] due to relatively easier market conditions, while high-cap projects face risks such as money laundering [3] and phishing scams [25], which have shown new forms and characteristics in DeFi. This taxonomy provides a systematic categorization of DeFi frauds based on their occurrence time, revealing the complex landscape of DeFi frauds.

With this taxonomy, our survey provides a comprehensive review of on-chain frauds and of existing fraud detection methods targeted at frauds that occur at each stage, leading to noteworthy findings and potential future directions across the life cycle of DeFi projects. Below are some highlights:

- • Fraud Types and Organizers: During the development stage, most frauds involve investment scams organized by project developers. As projects progress to the introduction and growth stages, market manipulations emerge, and project developers and DeFi platforms collaborate to organize fraudulent activities. In the maturity and decline stages, the role of fraud organizers shifts to external entities, who also collaborate with DeFi platforms to organize some market manipulations and new forms of illicit activities.

- • Detection Methods: During the development stage, tree-based models are prominent for fraud detection tasks because they have shown superior performance for the small data in this stage. In the introduction and growth stages, statistical methods and graph-based patterns are widely used to capture suspicious market activities. Advanced techniques, particularly graph-based methods, gain prominence in the maturity and decline stages to capture complex relationships in large and complex data.

- • Detection Effectiveness: For frauds that occur in the early stages, fraud detection tasks are still in the beginning phases, possibly due to limited transaction data and a scarcity of reliable ground truths. In comparison, frauds in the later stages have received significant attention, with good detection performance using a large amount of data and advanced models.

- • Future Directions: During the early stages, leveraging pre-trained models and conducting early-stage detection can aid in proactive fraud prevention. In the later phase, researchers can leverage large language models (LLM) or foundational models to gather more comprehensive information and develop advanced detection techniques. More future directions and open issues throughout the entire life cycle are also presented in this paper.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 and Section 3 provide a background on DeFi frauds and our motivation for this survey, respectively. Section 4 presents a DeFi fraud taxonomy and an overview of detection methods. Sections 5, 6 and 7 review stage-specific frauds and detection methods. Section 8 presents discussion and findings, and Section 9 discusses potential future directions. Finally, Section 10 concludes this paper.
